chapter_theme: Songs at Tiruvenkatam (வடமலை): the body's old age, the women's net, the fire of desire and the sea of sects, and Death taking the soul alone, against which the poet asks to serve the Lord's servants before the body ripens, to chant the six-syllable name and to escape hell; the praise, at Vishnu's hill, dwells on Murugan as nephew of Rama and Krishna.
structure_note: Every song names Vishnu's deeds in its praise, fitting the shrine: Rama at Lanka (524, 529), Krishna as Arjuna's charioteer (527, 529), Kaliya and Narasimha (526). 527 and 528 share their last two lines.

524.reading: The poet describes old age: black hair whitened, eyes sunken, cheeks dried, ears turned to skin, neck and back bent, teeth fallen, drool, a cough that shakes the bones at night, a cracked voice and a stick for a leg; before his body ripens so, he asks whether he will eagerly serve those who are Murugan's servants. The praise tells of Vishnu who brought back the Vedas from the sea, bridged the ocean, took Hanuman to his side and cut Ravana's ten heads with his bow, and names Murugan, with the vel in his lotus hand, his nephew, at the northern mountain.
524.nuance: உடம்பு பழுத்திடு முன், before the body ripens, puts the plea before old age, not at death. The service asked is to the Lord's servants (உனக்கடிமை படுமவர் தொண்டு), a step below serving the Lord himself.

525.reading: The poet asks that, chanting 'Saravanabhava, treasure, six-faced one, supreme guru' and melting in Tamil like the devotees, his birth and death end, he reach Sivam, his disease end and his life be well, and that one day he be given the shade of Murugan's feet so that the sufferings of creatures on the sea-girt earth may cease. The praise names Murugan as Ganapati's younger brother, who gives life to poets, who walks at Tanigai, Sivagiri and the northern mountain, who dispels the darkness of impurity from devotees' minds like the sun, nephew of Vishnu and Narasimha, son of Uma, on the peacock that shakes the nether worlds.
525.nuance: The opening repeats the formula சரவணபவ நிதி அறுமுக குருபர three times, so the song enacts the chanting it describes. The plea widens beyond the poet to all creatures (கடலுலகினில் வரும் உயிர்படும் அவதிகள்).

526.reading: The poet describes a woman's hair dense with flowers, bees and incense smoke and her forehead with its mark like Kama's or Indra's bow, and asks for grace for one who, drawn by these, gave up the true worship that says there is no refuge but Murugan's flower feet. The praise names Vishnu who danced on the serpent's hood, holds conch, discus and lotus and tore the night-demon, Murugan as his nephew with twelve shoulders, who fought the dark demon clans, at the northern mountain.
526.nuance: The plea turns on மெய் வழிபடல் ஒழிவனை, one who left off true worship, and its object, the feet as the only support (துணைப் பதமலர் அலது இலை). The rhythm compresses the words heavily and the split of the plea is uncertain.

527.reading: The poet speaks of desiring women's breasts, spear eyes, dark hair, bangled hands and mango-leaf bodies, unable to leave their union and wandering in great wrong, and asks not to die that way and fall into hell. The praise names Murugan who became a sage and a vengai tree to win the hunter girl, nephew of the one who drove the Pandavas' chariot, who told the Pandya king to wear holy ash, Lord of Venkatam where tigers, elephants and deer live, who gives his devotees whatever they ask.
527.nuance: நரகில் வீழ்ந்து அலையாமல், not to fall and toss in hell, is a rarer fear than Death in the book. பாண்டியன் நீறணிய மொழிவோனே again identifies Murugan with Sambandar, who brought the Pandya king to wear the ash.

528.reading: The poet tells how he could not swim the sea of quarrelling sects or quench the fire of desire, trusted worldly people as his help, and melted over women until his understanding failed, and asks whether it is right that he go alone into the power of Death, who takes the life as one wails. The praise names Valli of the forest, Murugan as Visakha and Saravana, Lord of the gods and of the Veda, husband of Devayanai, Guha and Senthan, at the Venkatam hill, who gives his devotees whatever they ask.
528.nuance: யான் தனி போய்விடுவது இயல்போதான், is it right that I go alone, is the plea: at death the friends trusted (உலகர் தாம் துணையாவர்) do not come. சமய விரோத சாங்கலை வாரி, the ocean of hostile sects, stands beside desire as the second thing the poet cannot cross.

529.reading: The poet asks to be spared drinking lip-nectar on the bed under women's fish-like eyes and dark hair, caught in their net and the illusion of their faces, and to be given the two feet so that 'mine' and 'theirs' fall away and the harsh frenzy of impurity and delusion ends. The praise names Krishna as the charioteer of the Pandavas against Duryodhana, the discus-bearer, and Rama who pierced Vali and the seven sal trees and shattered Ravana's ten heads, and Murugan as Guha, their nephew, at Tiruvenkatam.
529.nuance: எனதாம் தனதானவை போய் அற, that what is mine and what is theirs go, names attachment as the root beneath lust; மலமாம் கடு மோக விகாரம் makes the delusion itself an impurity.

links.note: Both look ahead to grey hair and the staff and draw the lesson that one should act before they come: the Naladiyar praises those who renounced in childhood, 524 asks to serve the Lord's servants before the body ripens.
The two songs end with the same two lines, Murugan dwelling on the Venkatam hill and giving his devotees whatever they ask when they ask it; a formula of this shrine.

source_issues: Song 527: வேங்யு மானும் (line 13) has a broken word, perhaps வேங்கையு or another animal name.
